item.statement_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix compact $(X,g)$, compact transverse boundary submanifolds $L_0,L_1$, and a smooth $J_t$ with fixed totally real boundary structures. Suppose fixed disjoint generator charts about their finite intersection identify the boundaries with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t$ with $i$ for every $t$. Fix end generators $x_-,x_+$ and $0\le\delta<\pi/2$, using a smooth weight $e^{\delta\rho(s)}$ as in the weighted Sobolev algebra lemma.

There is an actual second-countable separable real Hilbert configuration manifold $\mathcal B_\delta$ of strip maps with these boundary values and ends, constructed as the union of the following local charts. A reference map $u_0$ is smooth, satisfies the boundary condition, and equals $x_\pm$ outside a compact longitudinal interval. Its tangent model is
$$\mathcal X_{u_0}=H^3_\delta(u_0^*TX)\cap\mathcal X^1_{u_0},$$
where $\mathcal X^1_{u_0}$ is the $H^1$ completion of compactly supported smooth tangent sections satisfying $TL_0,TL_1$ on the edges. This is an intersection with the $H^1$ domain, not an asserted $H^3$ closure. Small sections give maps $u=\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)$ for the actual boundary-preserving local addition. All smooth finite-energy $J_t$ strips with these ends belong to this manifold.

The actual Cauchy–Riemann expression $u_s+J_t(u)u_t$ defines a smooth section of the Hilbert bundle with fiber $H^2_\delta(u^*TX)$. In the local-addition trivialization it is a smooth map $\mathcal F_{u_0}:\mathcal X_{u_0}\to H^2_\delta(u_0^*TX)$. On a small norm ball its nonlinear remainder obeys
$$\|\mathcal F(\xi)-\mathcal F(\eta)-D\mathcal F(0)(\xi-\eta)\|_{H^2_\delta}\le C(\|\xi\|_{H^3_\delta}+\|\eta\|_{H^3_\delta})\|\xi-\eta\|_{H^3_\delta}.$$
The constants are uniform for reference families with uniform coefficient/frame derivatives through the orders used in this estimate. Every zero is smooth and has finite energy and the prescribed ends. At each zero the derivative is the actual geometric Fredholm linearization $H^3_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1\to H^2_\delta$, with the same real index as its $H^1\to L^2$ realization, before translation quotient. No universal transversality or gluing is claimed.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: We first extend the algebra statement of [F2] to compositions in $H^3_\delta$. Its $H^3\subset C^1$ bound makes every first derivative bounded. The third-order product terms are $fD^3g$, $D^3f\,g$, $D^2f\,Dg$ and $Df\,D^2g$; each is $L^2$ using a bounded factor. Thus $H^3$ is an algebra. Weighted versions put the weight on one factor, as in [F2]. Third-order chain terms are a bounded coefficient times $D^3u$, $D^2u\,Du$, or three first derivatives, in addition to lower source-order terms. They have the same weighted $L^2$ bounds, putting at most one differentiated factor in $L^2$ and the others in $L^\infty$. The smooth approximation and Taylor proof of [F2] therefore applies verbatim at this order, with source coefficient derivatives through order three, proving smooth $H^3_\delta$ composition and multiplication. A coefficient's nonzero value at zero is treated as a bounded smooth multiplier, or as a fixed $H^3_\delta$ offset when compactly supported in $s$. All coefficient extensions used below have this latter offset property. [F2, construct, algebra]

The pointwise boundary condition for an $H^3$ section is equivalent to membership in the indicated $H^1$ boundary domain. In fixed product-line coordinates, the forward implication from completion to trace follows from the weak endpoint $L^2$ estimate proved in [F2]; a continuous $H^3$ representative with that trace lies in the closed real plane at every boundary point. Conversely cut a boundary-compatible $H^3$ section off in $s$ in the $H^1$ norm and split it by a real partition in $t$ into two edge pieces and an interior piece. At the lower edge extend the real part evenly and imaginary part oddly; matching real boundary values make this an $H^1$ extension, as verified by the weak primitive and integration-by-parts argument in [F2]. Convolve with a smooth kernel even in the normal variable. The resulting smooth maps have real boundary values and converge in $H^1$. At the upper edge rotate its line to the real line first, reflect about $t=1$, and use the same construction; its piece is supported away from the other edge. The interior piece is convolved away from both edges. Their sum is a compactly supported smooth boundary-compatible approximation in $H^1$. For the variable product planes from [F3] use its smooth scalar gauge first and undo it after approximation. This proves precisely the required $H^1$ membership, without identifying an $H^3$ closure or imposing normal traces. Scalar weights preserve these pointwise planes. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

The model spaces are separable Hilbert spaces. Use the smooth frame construction of [F3] for $u_0^*TX$; if desired its operator input can be chosen as $\nabla_s+J_t(u_0)\nabla_t$ for the connection in [F1], which is exactly $D_0$ on the constant flat ends. The frame and scalar gauge have bounded derivatives of every fixed order on a compact core and constant comparisons on the ends. They identify the model with a closed real subspace of ordinary weighted $H^3$: the extra $H^1$ domain is closed there. Multiplication by the smooth weight identifies weighted and unweighted Hilbert norms. For separability, split the strip into countably many unit rectangles. By [F5] finite Fourier sums with rational coefficients on finitely many such blocks are a countable dense subset of $L^2$. The graph $f\mapsto(D^\alpha f)_{|\alpha|\le3}$ embeds $H^3$ isometrically as a closed subspace of a finite sum of such $L^2$ spaces; closedness follows by passing weak derivative identities to $L^2$ limits against tests. A closed subspace of a Hilbert space has its orthogonal projection under Countable Choice: a minimizing sequence exists by that axiom and is Cauchy by the parallelogram identity; its unique limit is the nearest point and the usual orthogonality calculation gives a bounded linear projection. Project the countable ambient dense family to obtain a countable dense family in the graph, and then in the boundary subspace by the same argument. This proves the model assertion without an unrestricted-choice subspace theorem. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

For a small $H^3_\delta$ ball of $\xi\in\mathcal X_{u_0}$, [F2] makes its supremum small enough for [F1], so $u=\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)$ is a well-defined $C^1$ map with boundary in $L_j$. Both its value and first derivative approach the prescribed ends. For $\delta=0$ the decay follows by localizing the $H^3$ norm on unit longitudinal windows: their norms tend to zero on the tails by integrability, and the fixed local embedding bound in [F2] gives uniform $C^1$ decay. For positive weight the same estimate applies, or directly uses its exponential factor. References have constant ends, so the reference derivative is compactly supported. Thus $du\in L^2$ and the map has finite energy. The pointwise inverse local addition identifies the chart injectively. Conversely its coordinate inverse is $H^3_\delta$ whenever a second chart map is sufficiently close in this topology, by step 1.1 and bounded smooth finite-dimensional inverse coefficients. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Charts are smoothly compatible on their overlap. The transition formula is the pointwise expression $\eta=\mathcal E^{-1}_{u_1}(\mathcal E(u_0,\xi))$. Near any overlap map its finite-dimensional formula has uniform positive distance from the boundary of its definition domain. On the compact source core extend its smooth coefficients off that graph by finitely many ordinary smooth coordinate cutoffs; this is possible since the graph is compact and contained in an open coefficient domain. On the ends both references are the same constants and the local addition is linear, so the transition is a fixed linear coordinate change with zero offset. Thus step 1.1 gives a smooth $H^3_\delta$ transition near that map. Its pointwise boundary values lie in $T L_j$ by the inverse assertion of [F1]; by step 1.2 it therefore lies in exactly the other model $H^3_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1$, not a larger unproved domain. Its inverse has the same property. Smoothness restricts to these closed Hilbert subspaces because all derivatives are limits of difference quotients in the respective closed target space. This proves the local Hilbert atlas for the union of these actual chart images. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

A zero gives a continuous weak $W^{1,2}$ solution with totally real boundary, so [F4] makes it smooth up to the boundary. Finite energy and its prescribed ends were proved in step 3.1. Conversely every smooth finite-energy strip has the exponential all-order tails of [F4]. Truncate it sufficiently far out by a real cutoff in the exact product generator coordinates to obtain a smooth reference equal to $x_\pm$ on the ends, preserving both linear boundary planes. The inverse local-addition difference between this reference and the original map tends to zero in $H^3_\delta$ as the truncation moves out, because $\delta<\pi/2$ and the tails decay with that spectral rate. It is pointwise tangent on the boundary and thus belongs to the model by step 1.2. For large truncation the strip therefore lies in that actual chart, proving that all smooth finite-energy strips are included. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

This atlas is second-countable. An explicit finite-atlas embedding of $X$ is $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$, where $\phi_i$ is a finite smooth partition in coordinate charts; equality or differential vanishing recovers a point or tangent vector in a chart with $\phi_i>0$. Compactness makes it an embedding. Fix a smooth ambient reference $r(s,t)$ equal to $F(x_\pm)$ outside a compact interval. Map our configuration space into the separable Hilbert space $H^3_\delta(S;\mathbb R^N)$ by $u\mapsto F(u)-r$. The local composition estimates show this is continuous in each chart, injective, and has continuous local inverse on its image. For the last assertion, use the smooth inverse local addition and smooth local inverses of $F$ in finite relatively compact target charts; finite cutoffs give bounded coefficient extensions, so step 1.1 applies. Consequently each chart image is open in the subspace topology of this embedding: nearby configurations have an inverse coordinate close in $H^3_\delta$ and satisfy its boundary domain by step 1.2. A subspace of a second-countable metric space is second-countable, so this topology has a countable base. A countable chart subcover can be selected under Countable Choice by choosing one chart containing each basis element that is contained in some chart. This proves the stated configuration manifold properties. No assertion that every arbitrary pointwise constrained rough map has already been approximated in $H^3$ was used or needed. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Define the range bundle using $\mathcal T_\xi=d_v\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)^{-1}:u^*TX\to u_0^*TX$ and the fixed $H^2_\delta$ target in a chart. This inverse exists for the small sections by [F1]. Its coefficient and its inverse have the bounded smooth composition estimates of [F2]; transition multiplication is consequently a smooth bounded invertible $H^2_\delta$ operator depending smoothly on the $H^3_\delta$ chart variable. These are the actual Hilbert-bundle trivializations. In them the section is $$\mathcal F_{u_0}(\xi)=\mathcal T_\xi\bigl(\partial_s\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)+J_t(\mathcal E(u_0,\xi))\partial_t\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)\bigr).$$ The weak chain rule follows from the same smooth approximation as [F2]. In a smooth bundle frame this is a sum of smooth bounded coefficients in $(s,t,\xi)$ times $\xi_s,\xi_t$, and a zeroth-order term. The zeroth-order value at zero is smooth and compactly supported in $s$, because $u_0$ has constant ends. Its difference from that value vanishes at $\xi=0$. Thus [F2], step 1.1 and bounded differentiation $H^3_\delta\to H^2_\delta$ prove that this is a genuine smooth section in the asserted Hilbert bundle. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

The same formulas give the quadratic bound. Their first and second Frechet derivatives are finite sums of bounded smooth coefficient compositions, variations and first derivatives of variations; multiplication is controlled by the $H^2_\delta$ algebra and $H^3_\delta\to H^2_\delta$ differentiation in [F2]. On a fixed small norm ball the second derivative is bounded by a constant depending only on the finitely many coefficient and frame derivative bounds used there. The fundamental theorem along line segments then gives $$\|D\mathcal F(\zeta)-D\mathcal F(0)\|\le C\|\zeta\|_{H^3_\delta}.$$ Integrating from $\eta$ to $\xi$ gives exactly the displayed remainder estimate. This proof shows uniformity for reference families with the specified uniform bounds, rather than assuming a uniform nonlinear estimate as a moduli axiom. [F2, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

At a zero, differentiation of the section is its actual geometric linearization: in local target coordinates it is $P\xi=\xi_s+J_t(u)\xi_t+(dJ_t)_u[\xi]u_t$. Differentiating the range trivialization adds a factor times the section itself, which vanishes there. The same observation makes coordinate changes conjugate this derivative intrinsically. Far out on either end, the map lies in the fixed generator chart, where $J_t=i$ exactly and its target derivatives vanish, so the operator is exactly $D_0$ with the two product boundary planes. Its smooth coefficients and frames have bounded derivatives of all orders on the compact core and exponentially controlled ends by [F4]. All hypotheses of the actual geometric frame and higher Sobolev Fredholm results in [F3] therefore hold. At this smooth zero the pointwise derivative $d_v\mathcal E$ and its inverse have bounded smooth coefficients; they identify the chart tangent space with the actual geometric section space and carry its boundary tangent plane bijectively to $TL_j$, by differentiating the boundary-preserving local addition. Our domain is therefore exactly their $H^3_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1$, justified in step 1.2, and our range is their $H^2_\delta$. They give the asserted Fredholmness and common real index before translation quotient. This completes the actual configuration-space and section construction while leaving universal submersion and gluing as separate obligations. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 5.2, step 4.2, construct, algebra] ∎
